A model is a deliberately simplified, computable story about a phenomenon, and building one is a loop —
— with verification and validation being two different checks that beginners constantly confuse.

Every other chapter in this book builds a specific model: an epidemic curve, a diffusing particle, a stock price, a tournament bracket. This chapter is about the thing they have in common — the
of turning a messy real-world phenomenon into something you can compute with, and knowing how much to trust the answer.

A model is not the phenomenon. It is a chosen simplification: you throw away almost everything and keep the few features you think drive the behavior you care about. “The better team wins the World Series” is not a fact about baseball; it is a

you can only answer once you have committed to a model of what “better” means and how a series unfolds. The commitment is where the intellectual work lives, and it is exactly the part a coding agent will happily skip if you let it.

That last point matters more in this course than it used to. You will use coding agents to implement your models, and an agent is very good at producing plausible code fast. What it cannot do for you is decide
what you are willing to assume
how you would know if the answer were wrong

. Those three decisions are the model. This chapter is a framework for making them deliberately — before you prompt — and a running example, the baseball best-of-7 series, small enough to walk end to end.
We use very little new machinery here; the point is conceptual. The running example needs only:

Turn the structure into something computable — a formula, a simulation, a fitted routine. This is the stage a coding agent can do most of for you.
Check that the implementation faithfully computes the mathematics you specified.
Did I solve the equations I wrote down correctly?
Check that the model — assumptions and all — actually describes reality.
Did I write down the right equations?
Verification and validation both feed back into formulation. A failed verification means a bug; a failed validation means the
is wrong (or the question was), and you revise assumptions and go around again.
Every later chapter runs through these five stages once, on a harder phenomenon. The chapters differ in the mathematics; the sequence of steps does not.
Verification and validation: two different checks

children.label: Verification and validation: two different checks

children.value: These two words sound like synonyms and are not. Keeping them apart is one of the ideas the rest of the book depends on most, and this chapter is where the distinction is introduced; it comes back in force in the Monte Carlo & Estimation chapter and again in the Queuing chapter.
Verification: am I solving the equations right?
— a closed-form solution, a limiting case, a conservation law, an invariant. Verification never looks at real-world data. It asks only whether your code faithfully computes the model you specified.
Validation: am I solving the right equations?
— compare predictions to data the model was not built to reproduce, look at residual structure, test out-of-sample. Validation is the only stage that can tell you your assumptions are wrong.
verification is “did we build the thing right?”; validation is “did we build the right thing?”
You can have a perfectly verified implementation of a completely wrong model. That is the trap Worked Example 2 is built around.
Every model rests on assumptions, and they come in two kinds:
are the ones you write down: “games are independent,” “

children.html: ppp

children.value: is the same every game.” You can see them, so you can question them.

are the ones baked in silently by your modeling choices: that home-field advantage doesn’t matter, that pitching rotations don’t shift the win probability from game to game, that no player gets injured mid-series, that both teams try equally hard in every game. You didn’t decide these; you just failed to

The dangerous assumptions are almost always the implicit ones, because you can’t validate against a possibility you never noticed. A coding agent is especially prone to adding implicit assumptions without telling you — it will pick a reasonable-looking default and not mention that it chose one. Half of “modeling judgment” is surfacing implicit assumptions and promoting them to explicit ones so they can be checked.
This is an agent-era course. You will hand implementation to a coding agent constantly, and you should. But the agent operates
step 2 of the loop; the value you add is steps 1, 3, and 4. So before you type a prompt, do the pre-agent thinking on paper:

a prompt should encode a question and its checks, not just a request for code.

An agent that is told the limiting case and the validation target will write better code and you will catch its mistakes. An agent handed “simulate the World Series” will confidently return something, and you will have no independent way to know if it’s right.

A century of baseball sounds like a lot of data, and for this question it is not. To have an 80% chance of detecting a gap of even 5.75 points — the discrepancy people usually claim is there — you would need about 530 series, roughly 4.6 times the entire history of the event. That is the real lesson, and it is a validation result: you compared against a number the model did not choose, and learned that the comparison is inconclusive. Reporting the 3.5-point gap as evidence of a modelling failure would be exactly the overreach this chapter is about.

How to tell which one you did.

If the check uses only quantities you put into the model, it is verification. If it uses a number from the outside world that the model had no say in, it is validation. A simulation is your assumptions executed, so it can never validate the assumptions it was built from.
If verification never uses data, what good is it?
Verification catches the enormous class of errors where your

— off-by-one bugs, wrong array indexing, a sign error, an agent that quietly changed your specification. Those bugs are invisible to validation (a buggy implementation of a good model can look “close enough” to data and hide the bug). You verify first so that when validation fails, you know it’s the
Why can’t a simulation validate my model?

Because a simulation is just your assumptions, executed. It can only tell you what your assumptions imply — never whether your assumptions are true. Matching a simulation to a formula built from the same assumptions checks the two computations against each other, and both of them encode the same assumptions, so neither can test those assumptions. Validation requires an
source of truth: real data the model did not get to see.
Isn’t the best-of-7 “better team wins” answer just... the answer?

Every model output carries an implicit “...assuming the model is right,” and a good modeler says that clause out loud. The number is a claim about the model; validation is what upgrades it (partially) to a claim about the world.
Why do the pre-agent thinking if the agent writes the code anyway?
Because the agent operates only inside the

step. It cannot choose your question, cannot know which implicit assumptions you’re willing to accept, and cannot invent a validation check against data it’s never seen. If you skip formulation and checks, you’ve delegated the two stages an agent
do and abandoned the three it
— and you’ll accept plausible-looking wrong answers because you built no way to catch them.

For each check below, say whether it is verification or validation, and why. (a) Your epidemic simulation conserves total population at every timestep. (b) Your epidemic model’s predicted case curve is compared to reported case counts from a city it wasn’t fit on. (c) Your option-pricing code reproduces the Black–Scholes formula in the zero-volatility limit. (d) A colleague reruns your Monte Carlo with a different seed and gets a statistically consistent answer. (e) Your traffic model predicts stop-and-go waves, and dashcam footage shows them.

opponent’s free-throw make probability is known/estimable (explicit); no offensive rebounds off a missed second free throw (implicit, and false); the leading team can inbound and be fouled without a turnover (implicit); clock/possession dynamics reduce to a fixed number of opponent possessions (explicit simplification).

compare the model’s recommended strategy against play-by-play data on teams that actually fouled vs. didn’t. But note this is

: coaches choose to foul in particular situations, so the two groups differ in more than the strategy — score, time remaining, foul counts, opponent free-throw quality. A raw comparison of win rates measures the selection as much as the tactic. To make it a real validation you would need to match on game state (or otherwise adjust for it), and even then you should report it as suggestive rather than causal.
